title: Knowledge Check 10: Lessons 73-80
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 73-80 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A Message Router receives one message and must deliver it to one of several channels. What discipline keeps it a router rather than a router and translator combined?
options: It decides the destination only and forwards the payload unchanged.
It rewrites the payload into the target format before forwarding it.
It merges several related messages into one combined payload first.
It holds the message until every downstream channel confirms receipt.
questions.explanation: A router answers only where a message goes; reshaping the payload belongs to a separate translator, which keeps routing rules simple and testable.

questions.question: Two systems integrate today and four more will join next year, each needing its own mapping. Why does a canonical data model reduce the maintenance burden?
options: It forces every system onto one binary wire format, so no mapping is needed again.
It only helps when exactly two systems integrate, so it suits small point-to-point links.
It turns many pairwise mappings into one per system, so the count grows additively.
It removes the need for translators by making every system share a single database.
questions.explanation: Mapping every source to every target grows multiplicatively, while mapping each system to one shared contract grows additively and stays maintainable as systems join.

questions.question: A quoting flow fans a request out to several providers and needs a usable rate quickly, where waiting for every reply would be too slow. Which aggregator design fits?
options: Send every provider reply to its own queue without combining them.
Stop at the first acceptable reply, matched to the request by a correlation key.
Wait for every provider reply before publishing, no matter how long it takes.
Translate each reply into a shared format and publish each reply to its own channel.
questions.explanation: An aggregator needs a correlation key and an explicit completeness condition; stopping at the first acceptable reply trades completeness for latency, which matches a quote.

questions.question: An architecture splits its code into many independently deployable services, but every service still wires directly to every partner. Which axis of the design changed, and which did not?
options: The code-splitting axis changed but the topology axis did not, so the point-to-point wiring remains.
The topology axis changed because services that deploy independently always form a hub.
Both axes changed, because splitting code into services removes the need for any mediator between systems.
Neither axis changed, because the number of services does not affect integration shape.
questions.explanation: Code shape and topology are independent decisions; distributing the code into services says nothing about whether anything mediates the connections between systems.

questions.question: An ERP owns the authoritative customer master, and Salesforce only holds a synced copy for its sales team. What role does Salesforce actually play?
options: The hub, because any synced copy of the master counts as the system of record.
The hub, because the sales team reads the customer record most often.
A spoke; calling it the hub is honest only if the system of record moves to it.
A hub already, as long as a sync keeps the local copy fresh enough to trust for daily sales work.
questions.explanation: The system-of-record test asks where the authoritative copy lives; converging traffic at a copy that can drift is a different design from owning the truth.

questions.question: Salesforce is proposed as the integration hub for a high-volume process. Why must the design treat governor and API limits as an architectural constraint?
options: Because resource limits reset automatically and apply only to sandbox environments.
Because each transaction and each day has a finite budget, so volume belongs on async paths.
Because limits apply only to Apex code and never to declarative automation, flows, or integrations.
Because limits can be raised on request for any org without changing its license mix.
questions.explanation: A multitenant hub concentrates traffic into a governed, finite budget, so high-volume work belongs on event-driven and batched paths designed to a healthy fraction of the limits.

questions.question: Which contrast correctly separates an agent from a workflow?
options: A workflow uses several models, while an agent uses only one.
A workflow follows fixed code paths, while an agent lets the model choose steps at runtime.
A workflow cannot call tools at all, while an agent always calls at least one tool during its run.
A workflow runs on a server, while an agent runs on the end user's device.
questions.explanation: In a workflow the control flow lives in code, while an agent lets the model decide at runtime which tool to call and whether to continue, so the control flow lives partly in the model.

questions.question: When designing the tool surface for an agent, which practice most improves the reliability of tool use?
options: Add more tools to the catalog so the model has more options at each step.
Describe each tool in the shortest possible terms to keep the whole prompt as small as possible.
Rely on the model to remember subtle rules about how each tool behaves.
Shape each tool's arguments and description so a likely mistake is hard to make.
questions.explanation: Shaping a tool so a likely mistake is impossible to make works better than telling the model to remember a rule, because the interface itself prevents the error.

questions.question: A client asks for a multi-agent architecture for a task one agent already handles. What is the disciplined first response?
options: Start single and split only when one agent is the bottleneck, because splitting multiplies cost.
Start multi-agent immediately, because parallel subagents always lower the total tokens spent per task.
Start multi-agent immediately, because one agent cannot call tools more than once per run.
Start with a fixed workflow, because agents cannot be traced or evaluated in production.
questions.explanation: A single agent is simpler to evaluate and maintain; multi-agent designs multiply tokens and coordination surface, so a split has to be earned by a real bottleneck.

questions.question: Which principle should guide an architect who wants to lower API consumption for a nightly data load?
options: Cost scales with record count, so splitting the load into more calls lowers the bill.
Cost scales with named users, so only seat count changes consumption.
Cost scales with the call, so batching records into fewer calls lowers the bill.
Cost scales with storage volume, so only archiving changes consumption.
questions.explanation: The unit of cost is the call, not the record; a bulk job or composite request carries many records per call, which is why it costs far less than one call per record.

questions.question: A support agent carries a large pasted context on every turn. Why does trimming that context cut the AI bill by whole multiples?
options: Billing rounds prompt size up in fixed token blocks, so crossing a block boundary drops whole units.
Billing charges only for output tokens, so shorter input context has no effect on cost.
Billing multiplies by the number of actions, so context size changes the action count.
Billing charges the context once per conversation, so trimming it has no effect on the recurring bill.
questions.explanation: Prompt billing is per block of up to 2,000 tokens rounded up, so a smaller context can cross a block boundary and bill one unit instead of several.

questions.question: A large group of users only reads cases and updates one status field. Which licensing approach fits that usage?
options: Buy the top license tier for everyone, because a lower tier blocks all record updates and reports.
Use a lower base license and grant the few extra capabilities with permission set licenses.
Use community licenses for internal staff, because they carry the same feature ceiling.
Skip permission sets and widen the profile, because permission sets cannot grant features.
questions.explanation: The base license sets the ceiling and permission set licenses raise it for specific people, so read-mostly users do not need a full seat to get the few capabilities they use.

questions.question: An org compares average API usage to its allocation and concludes it has plenty of room. Why is that conclusion unsafe?
options: Because average usage is always higher than peak usage, so the comparison overstates risk.
Because headroom must be measured at peak, and an average hides the hour the limit is hit.
Because the allocation is recalculated hourly, so any single comparison is already stale.
Because API limits rarely bind, so almost any measurement of usage is optional.
questions.explanation: Headroom is only meaningful at peak; an average can look comfortable while the busiest hour is already near the ceiling.

questions.question: A list view on a very large object has slowed sharply, and someone proposes buying more capacity. What should be checked first?
options: Whether more allocation would speed up the query, since scans are only a capacity problem.
Whether the view could become a scheduled report, since list views cannot use indexes.
Whether the object could become a Big Object, since that fixes interactive latency at any volume.
Whether a non-selective filter forces a scan, which extra capacity cannot speed up.
questions.explanation: The decision rule asks first whether the constraint is consumed by waste; a scan caused by a non-selective filter is a design problem that buying capacity does not fix.

questions.question: A batch finishes comfortably in a full copy sandbox but takes much longer in production. What does the sandbox result actually establish?
options: It establishes data-volume behavior only, not concurrency or overlapping job schedules.
It establishes production capacity, because a full copy holds production-like data volumes.
It establishes concurrency behavior, because the sandbox serves the same user mix.
It establishes peak behavior, because the sandbox reproduces the month-end load.
questions.explanation: A sandbox proves data-volume behavior; it does not reproduce the real user mix, the overlapping job schedule, or shared-infrastructure effects, so its timing is a floor rather than a prediction.

questions.question: A release process cannot carry its intake, so teams bundle unrelated work into single changes and label more requests urgent. What is the underlying defect?
options: The windows are not frequent enough, so the fix is to add overtime weekend windows.
Deployment speed is the constraint, so the fix is faster validation and deployment tooling.
Two risk classes share one pipe, so low-risk work needs a separate, more frequent lane.
Request intake is simply too high, so the fix is to ask the business for fewer requests.
questions.explanation: Bundling and emergency inflation are symptoms of routing low-risk and high-risk work through the same narrow window; a separate standard lane removes the overload.

questions.question: Salesforce applies production upgrades on a fixed schedule the org does not control. How should a delivery plan treat those dates?
options: Plan backward from the published dates and test critical paths in preview.
Plan forward from the backlog and treat the upgrade like any scheduled release.
Postpone the upgrade to a quieter quarter, since production upgrades can be deferred.
Skip preview testing, because the upgrade is zero downtime and cannot break anything.
questions.explanation: The dates are published a year ahead and cannot be deferred, so the only sound move is to schedule backward from them and use the preview window to test critical paths.

questions.question: An org adds more all-change freezes around quarter end and around each release. Why can more freezes raise risk instead of lowering it?
options: Because a freeze also pauses vendor package updates and certificate expiry for its period.
Because a freeze removes the need for any rollback or forward-fix plan while it lasts.
Because a freeze forces every change to emergency tier and lengthens the normal path.
Because freezes squeeze work into narrower bands, so batch sizes grow and risk rises.
questions.explanation: Restricting more dates pushes the same work into fewer windows, which grows batch size and blast radius; a freeze works better when it blocks a specific risk class and leaves a standard lane open.

questions.question: Why are accepted decision records kept immutable instead of being edited when circumstances change?
options: Because rewriting an accepted record is the fastest way to keep the log aligned with practice.
Because editing erases what the team believed at the time, which the log exists to preserve.
Because records must stay accepted until the system they describe is retired.
Because a superseded record can be read only by its original author afterward.
questions.explanation: A log answers what the team believed on a specific date; changing an accepted record destroys that history, while a new record that supersedes it keeps both current truth and past reasoning.

questions.question: A large design document is accurate at sign-off and stale a year later. What structural change keeps documentation current?
options: Write a longer design document and review it once at each project milestone.
Keep the document as the single source and update it whenever someone remembers.
Store every decision in a wiki the team can edit freely after each release.
Keep one small record per decision in version control and gate the change on it.
questions.explanation: Small records are cheap to maintain and a merge gate makes updating them part of delivery, so the documentation cannot silently fall behind the system.

questions.question: Every decision record includes a revisit trigger. What does that trigger add?
options: It reopens the decision when its assumptions expire instead of leaving it settled.
It schedules the record for deletion once the decision has been in force for a year.
It lists the alternatives that were rejected, without needing the surrounding context.
It replaces the need for a named owner, because the trigger is what watches the record.
questions.explanation: A trigger turns a static record into an instrument that reports when its assumptions no longer hold, so a dated decision becomes a scheduled review instead of an accepted-forever default.

questions.question: Why does a deployed AI system need a system card in addition to a card for each model it uses?
options: Because a model card cannot name the training data when the model comes from a vendor.
Because a model card stops being accurate as soon as the next code commit is deployed.
Because routing, retrieval, tools, and permissions are system facts no card covers.
Because a system card removes the need to keep any per-model evaluation evidence.
questions.explanation: A model card describes one model, while the behavior of a deployed system comes from routing, retrieval, tools, prompts, and permissions that only a system card records.

questions.question: A draft system card claims prompts are protected by a platform control the vendor advertises. Why is that claim unsafe?
options: A card must record configured behavior for that surface, where the control may be off.
A card may restate any platform capability, since platforms enable every control by default.
A card only needs the model snapshot, because guardrails are documented by the vendor.
A card should list every capability the platform offers, whether or not the org uses it.
questions.explanation: A system card records what is actually configured on the surface in question; copying a platform capability without checking it can state a control that is disabled there.

questions.question: What is the purpose of comparing live configuration to the system card each quarter?
options: To confirm the card is filed in the repository beside the metadata.
To catch configuration that changed without the card, the case that causes incidents.
To measure how many documents the team has written against its annual coverage target.
To prove the model vendor shipped no new version during the quarter.
questions.explanation: A stale card is a maintenance problem, but a configuration change nobody documented leaves the running system unknown to the people accountable for it, which is what the diff catches.
